title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) comparing two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for end‑to‑end correctness. The preregistered design used shared_initial_candidate semantics so each pair received one identical LLM candidate (one shared generation per pair). Execution: 120 paired tasks (planned episodes 240, completed episodes 240), one shared generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, because generation was shared, the confirmatory test measures validator‑acceptance parity of identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness; preregistered hypotheses about independent generator/repair superiority (H1,H2) are therefore not testable in this execution. We provide artifact‑grounded evidence (execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces), confirm that no repairs were applied (repair_applied = false for all 240 episodes), and discuss minimal preregistered design changes required to discriminate architectures in follow‑ups.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is a pressing operational problem: constrained translators with formal verification can offer strong device‑level guarantees, while agentic LLM pipelines promise flexibility and repair. We posed the preregistered research question: for intent‑driven changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (reachability and policy isolation): (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The study was preregistered as CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 and executed with deterministic artifact capture. Important preregistered semantic: shared_initial_candidate—each paired task used one identical LLM candidate delivered to both arms. This design intentionally removes generator variance and therefore makes the run a measurement of downstream deterministic validator acceptance of identical candidates, not a direct comparison of independent generation or repair robustness. We therefore report (i) a fully archived paired execution that documents validator acceptance parity under shared_candidate semantics, (ii) exact artifact‑grounded outcomes and statistical diagnostics for the degenerate paired result, and (iii) precise minimal preregistered design changes required to produce a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison.
sections.related_work: Two streams frame this work. Formal translation→verification systems constrain outputs and apply deterministic checks to produce high‑assurance device changes [10,11,12,13]. Recent work on LLM‑based NetOps and agentic AIOps highlights flexible generation, guarded workflows, and the need for deterministic validators, but documents hallucination and repair challenges [5,6]. Prior studies rarely combine preregistration, paired designs, and artifactized deterministic validation; our contribution is a narrowly scoped, artifact‑backed methodological instance that clarifies what a shared_candidate paired execution can reveal about validator acceptance.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen design. The study preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) froze the paired estimand: paired difference in binary end‑to‑end operational correctness (A − B) over n = 120 paired intent tasks balanced by vendor×topology clusters (preregistered distribution: 3 vendors × 3 topology classes with the planned assignment noted in the preregistration). Key declared artifacts: generation model declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini, validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5, adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution semantics (preregistered and implemented): shared_initial_candidate (one LLM generation shared across both arms per pair), one allowed repair iteration per task if triggered. Primary outcome: binary correctness = 1 when deterministic validator accepted the final configuration and emulator reachability/isolation checks passed; otherwise 0. Analysis methods: paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) and exact two‑sided McNemar test implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1. Planned vs actual accounting. Preregistered planned episodes = 240 (120 pairs × 2 conditions). Execution manifest shows completed episodes = 240 and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Planned power assumed independent generation variance (used to motivate N = 120 for detecting ≈15pp difference), but the implemented shared_candidate semantics remove independent generation variance; thus the preregistered power calculation does not apply to this execution. Artifact references (representative, short prefixes): paired contingency table: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (hash prefix 9f25790c); condition summary: analysis/condition_summary.csv (9c77c96f); execution accounting and raw results: execution/raw_results.jsonl (c5b16909) and execution/model_configuration.json (1acce925). Per‑task validator traces and normalized configurations: execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json (0f2a74a6) and sibling files. Repair detection: analysis/missingness_summary.csv (be8cd717) and execution/scoring/*.json show repair_applied=false for all episodes.
sections.results: Execution outcome. The run completed with planned episodes 240, completed 240, failed 0, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Marginal success rates: baseline = 120/120 (100.0%); guarded = 120/120 (100.0%). Primary estimate: paired difference (A − B) = 0.00. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Repair outcomes. Aggregated repair_applied count = 0 for all 240 episodes (no repair loops executed); therefore preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage and repair iterations are unobserved in this execution and provide no evidence to compare repair efficacy between architectures. The authoritative numeric artifacts appear in analysis/results.json and the CSV files cited above.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and constraints. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics both pipelines received identical LLM candidates and the deterministic validator accepted those candidates in every case: the run measures validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates, not independent architectural robustness. The absence of discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0) produces a degenerate paired distribution; bootstrap CIs and McNemar p reflect that degeneracy (CI pinned at 0.00; p = 1.0). The preregistered power plan assumed independent generation variance and thus is not applicable to this shared_candidate execution—this mismatch is recorded in the preregistration and execution manifests. Repairs were not observed (repair_applied = false), so H2 and all repair‑related secondary hypotheses were not evaluated by the data. Practical implications. The artifact bundle documents a reproducible protocol for measuring validator acceptance parity when generation is held constant; this is useful for validator regression testing and for verifying deterministic verifier behavior across different orchestration wrappers. However, it does not support claims of translator vs agentic superiority in independent generation or repair robustness. Minimal preregistered design changes to produce a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison (each change maps to manifestable differences): (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm issues independent LLM generations per pair (model_calls_used would increase to 240 for initial candidates alone); (ii) allow multiple independent sampled generations per arm per task or multi‑model sampling to expose generator variance; (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied>0 can be observed and compared; (iv) increase device fidelity (hardware images or higher‑fidelity emulation) to reduce simulator‑to‑device contamination risk. Each proposed change is directly testable and would appear in the archived manifest (increased model_calls_used, nonzero repair_applied counts, additional provider_call events).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifactized paired comparison of translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines across 120 intent task pairs using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics both pipelines accepted the identical LLM candidates for all tasks, yielding 100% success in each arm (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), paired difference 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs occurred (repair_applied = false for all 240 episodes); consequently preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage/iterations are unobserved. The run therefore documents validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent architectural robustness; we list precise minimal preregistered protocol modifications that would enable a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in future work. All principal numbers and representative validator traces are archived in the execution and analysis manifests referenced above.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics were preregistered and used; this intentionally removes variance from the generation stage and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.
Task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
Single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
